title: Choosing linen for needlework
subtitle: Why linen ages better than cotton and how to work with its irregular surface.
excerpt: Linen is the traditional needlework ground for samplers and heirloom pieces. It is harder to count than Aida, has a slightly irregular surface from natural fibre slubs, and rewards slower, more deliberate stitching.
sourceNotes:
Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Fabric selection and linen notes.
Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), Internet Archive. Linen fabric types and preparation.

glossaryTerms.definition: A slight thickening or irregularity in the surface of a linen thread, caused by natural variation in the flax fibre. Slubs are normal and do not affect the count or the finished piece.
The thread count of a linen fabric, given as threads per inch. Cross-stitch on linen is worked over two threads, so 32-count linen gives 16 effective stitches per inch.

content.text: Linen has been the ground for needlework samplers since at least the seventeenth century, and with reason: it ages without yellowing, holds its shape under repeated washing, and grows softer over time. The
surface is part of the look, not a defect. The trade-off is that individual threads are harder to count than Aida squares, particularly under artificial light.
28-count embroidery linen: stitched over two threads, gives 14 effective stitches per inch. The step-up from 28-count evenweave for those who want the character of linen without a finer count.
32-count embroidery linen: stitched over two threads, gives 16 effective stitches per inch. The
36-count and 40-count embroidery linen: miniature work. One strand of floss, daylight lamp, magnifier. Not for beginners.

Pre-wash and press linen before beginning any project. This removes the sizing applied at the mill and pre-shrinks the cloth so the finished piece doesn't distort when washed later. Wash in cool water, roll in a towel to remove excess water, and press damp while still slightly moist.

Use a daylight lamp on linen: the individual threads are smaller than on Aida, and the colour of the cloth can mask thread count errors under warm or dim light. A magnifier loupe is useful at 32-count and above. Linen works best in a scroll frame or Q-snap, since a wooden hoop leaves ring marks that are very hard to remove from this cloth.

items.symptom: The finished piece puckers after washing
items.cause: The linen was not pre-washed, so it shrank unevenly once the piece was cleaned.
items.fix: Pre-wash all linen before stitching. If the piece is already finished, wash it gently and block it flat to dry under slight tension.

items.symptom: Miscounts appear that were not visible during stitching
items.cause: A slub in the linen was mistaken for two threads and counted as one.
items.fix: Work under a daylight lamp. Check the count periodically against a known start position.

content.text: Linen is the fabric of the sampler tradition and the surface embroidery revival. Knowing how to select and prepare it is the
skill that opens every historical reproduction pattern.
